07 · Q4 Pulse 3: draft codebooks for participants’ first messages

What people first asked an AI about their health (topic), and what kind of help they wanted (type of request)

Denicia Aragon Espinosa

November 05, 2026

In short

  • What changed. We now code only each participant’s first message to the AI, which is what they asked about before the AI’s answers steered the conversation. This means no code can be about “replying to the AI”.
  • Two separate codebooks.
    1. Health topic: what the message is about, such as a condition, a body system or an area of health. Each message gets one main (primary) topic and, if needed, one secondary topic.
    2. Type of request: what kind of help the person wanted from the AI. One message can ask for more than one kind of help.
  • How. For each codebook, an LLM (Claude Opus 5.5, the model running this coding session) read all 53 first messages 3 separate times. Each time it used a different random order and had no memory of the other passes. A 4th fresh session merged the three lists, keeping only codes found in at least 2 of the 3 passes.
  • Exclusions. 1 chat (69c41892) was excluded after the passes: it was a pasted homework assignment, not a personal health conversation. The passes saw it, but it is left out of every count, kappa and example below, so the results describe 52 first messages (section 4).
  • Your review decisions. After reading the draft you made 6 documented changes: “Help with a text task” was dropped, a Mental health and stress topic was added, and 3 messages were recoded (section 4). The LLM passes were not rerun.
  • Result.
    • Health topic: 11 topics (Fleiss’ kappa on the primary topic = 0.81).
    • Type of request: 6 types (median kappa per type = 0.92).
    • Codes under the 3-chat minimum: T11 Mental health and stress (2 chats; kept because you asked for it).
  • Quote check. 199 of 199 example quotes were found word for word in the participant’s first message.
  • Next step: your review. Read the two draft codebooks (sections 7 and 8) and edit them. Then we pilot them, freeze them, and code every first message 3 times.

Every prompt, input file and raw LLM output is saved in output/07_build-codebook/, so each step can be checked.

Why we changed the approach

Why first messages only? The first message shows what the person came to the AI for, in their own words, before the AI said anything. Later messages are mostly reactions to the AI’s answers (“thanks”, “what about the second one?”). In the earlier draft (all messages, see below), several codes described these follow-ups. Here we want to focus on what people asked about at first, so we code the first message only.

Why two codebooks? A single first message answers two different questions:

  • What is it about? “My knee hurts when I climb stairs” is about joints or pain. That is the health topic.
  • What do they want back? The same message could ask “why is this happening?”, “what should I do?” or “is this serious?”. That is the type of request.

Keeping the two apart means a topic code never has to say anything about the kind of help wanted, and the other way round. It also lets us cross the two later, for example to see which kinds of help people want for each topic.

Why an LLM-drafted codebook and not topic modeling? Topic modeling, such as LDA or BERTopic, is a statistical method that groups texts by which words they share. We did not use it here for three reasons:

  1. Too little data. Topic models need hundreds or thousands of texts to find stable groups. We have 52 messages.
  2. Too short. Half of the first messages have 18 words or fewer. Short texts share too few words for word-based grouping to work well.
  3. It can’t separate types of request. Topic models group by subject words such as “knee” or “rash”. They cannot tell “why is this happening?” from “what should I do?”, because those differ in what is asked, not in which health words appear.

A codebook built by reading, with definitions, examples and a check across 3 independent passes, works with small data. It is also transparent: you can read and edit every rule.

The earlier draft is kept for the record. The first draft coded prompting approaches across all participant messages. Its outputs, report and inputs are in output/07_build-codebook/old_all-messages/, and its scripts and prompts are in scripts/07_build-codebook/old_all-messages/. Its inputs and raw LLM outputs contain names, so don’t share them. That folder also holds the check of the 7 pastes with no participant message: all 7 are AI-only, so they have no first message and are not coded here.

1. Preparing the first messages

Script: scripts/07_build-codebook/07a_prepare_coding_input.py

  1. We started from the de-identified long file from step 05b, where personal names are replaced with [NAME]. We kept the 53 chats with at least 1 participant message. (One of these was excluded later; see section 4.)
  2. From each chat we took the participant’s first message (turn human_1). In 2 chats, the paste started with AI text before the participant’s first message (turn ai_0). There, that AI text is shown above the message, clearly labelled context only, do not code, because the first message makes little sense without it.
  3. Identifiers. We searched again for emails, ZIP codes and street addresses and found 0.
  4. Six shuffled copies. We made 3 copies of the messages for each codebook, each in its own random order (fixed seeds: topic 7101, 7102, 7103; request 7201, 7202, 7203). A different reading order stops the first few messages from shaping every pass the same way. The seeds let us rebuild the orders exactly (input/pass_orders.csv).
p_len <- ggplot(first_msg, aes(n_words)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.15, fill = project_colors["clay"], color = "white", boundary = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(first_msg$n_words), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed",
             color = project_colors["charcoal"]) +
  annotate("text", x = median(first_msg$n_words) * 1.15, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, size = 6.5,
           label = paste0("median = ", median(first_msg$n_words), " words"), color = project_colors["charcoal"]) +
  labs(title = "Most first messages are short",
       subtitle = "Words in each participant's first message (log scale)",
       x = "Words in the first message", y = "Messages")
p_len

save_fig("first-message-length", p_len, width = 11, height = 5.5)

2. Three independent passes per codebook

Script: scripts/07_build-codebook/07b_write_pass_prompts.py fills in prompts/topic_pass_prompt.md and prompts/request_pass_prompt.md once for each pass.

Each of the 6 passes ran in a separate, fresh LLM session. It could see only its own prompt and its own shuffled file, so no pass saw another pass’s answers. The rules in the prompts:

  • Health topic: code the subject only, not the kind of help wanted or who it is for. Give one primary topic and an optional secondary topic. Messages with no clear health subject get “NONE”.
  • Type of request: code the kind of help wanted, not the subject. A message can have several types. There is no code for replying to or following up on the AI.
  • Both: no example categories were given, so the codes come from the messages themselves. Each code needs a definition, signs, how it differs from its nearest code, 2–3 verbatim quotes, and at least 3 messages. We aimed for roughly 5–8 codes.

What each pass found:

bind_rows(topic$pass_codes |> mutate(book = "Health topic"),
          request$pass_codes |> mutate(book = "Type of request")) |>
  arrange(book, pass, desc(n_chats)) |>
  mutate(group = paste0(book, ": pass ", pass)) |>
  select(group, name, n_chats, merged_into) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "group") |>
  cols_label(name = "Code named by the pass", n_chats = "Messages", merged_into = "Merged into") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(16), row_group.font.weight = "bold")

Health topic

You are a qualitative researcher drafting a codebook from real data. This is pass 1 of 3 independent passes. Work only from the file named below. Do not open any other file in the project, and do not look for or read the output of any other pass.

## The data

`C:\Users\DeniciaAragon\OneDrive - Healogix\Q4_3_Pulse\output\07_build-codebook\input\topic_pass_1_input.txt` holds 53 short texts. Each one is the **first message** that a survey participant wrote to an AI chatbot about a health question, for themselves or for someone else. The messages appear in a shuffled order (seed 7101).

- Each block starts with `=== CHAT <chat_id> ===` and ends with `=== END CHAT ===`.
- `[FIRST MESSAGE]:` is the participant's first message. **This is the only text you code.**
- In 2 blocks, a `[CONTEXT ONLY ...]` line shows AI text that came before the first message. Read it only to understand what the message is about. Never code it or quote it.
- Line breaks were lost in the survey export, so text may run together. Personal names were replaced with `[NAME]`.

`C:\Users\DeniciaAragon\miniconda3\python.exe -c "print(open(r'C:\Users\DeniciaAragon\OneDrive - Healogix\Q4_3_Pulse\output\07_build-codebook\input\topic_pass_1_input.txt',encoding='utf-8').read())"`

## What to find

Build a codebook of **health topics**: the health subject each first message asks about, such as a condition, a body system, or an area of health.

- Code the **subject only**. Do not code what kind of answer the person wanted, who the question is about, or how it was phrased. A separate codebook covers the type of request.
- No example categories are given on purpose. The topics should come from the messages themselves.
- Give every message **one primary topic**, the main subject. Add **one optional secondary topic** only if the message clearly also asks about a second subject.
- Topics should be broad enough to recur. Keep only topics that cover at least 3 different messages, counting primary and secondary. For 53 messages, roughly 5 to 8 topics is a sensible size. Do not force a number.
- If a message has no clear health subject, or its subject fits none of your topics, give it the primary topic `"NONE"` and explain why in `no_code_chats`.

For each topic, give:

1. `name`: a short, plain-language name of 1 to 5 words.
2. `definition`: 1 to 3 sentences. The first sentence must stand on its own as the definition. Say what is included and what is not.
3. `signs`: 2 to 5 concrete signs in the message, such as kinds of words, conditions, body parts or medicines.
4. `closest_other`: the name of your most similar topic, and `how_it_differs` in one or two sentences, including how to decide between them.
5. `examples`: 2 or 3 example quotes from **different chats**, each with its `chat_id`. Each quote must be copied **exactly, character for character**, from a `[FIRST MESSAGE]` line: one continuous stretch of 3 to 40 words, or the whole message if it is shorter. Do not fix spelling, punctuation or capitals, and do not join separate pieces with "...".

## Output

Write **only** valid JSON, in UTF-8, to `C:\Users\DeniciaAragon\OneDrive - Healogix\Q4_3_Pulse\output\07_build-codebook\passes\topic_pass_1_raw_output.json`, with this exact structure:

```json
{
  "codebook": "topic",
  "pass": 1,
  "seed": 7101,
  "n_messages_read": 53,
  "codes": [

      "name": "...",

  "notes": "Anything a researcher should know: borderline calls, topics seen in only 1-2 messages, any personal identifiers you noticed."
}
```

`assignments` must hold all 53 chats exactly once. Every `primary` and `secondary` must be one of your topic names, `"NONE"` (primary only), or `null` (secondary only).

- Each block starts with `=== CHAT <chat_id> ===` and ends with `=== END CHAT ===`.
- `[FIRST MESSAGE]:` is the participant's first message. **This is the only text you code.**

## What to find

Build a codebook of **types of request**: what the participant wanted the AI to give them in this first message, that is, the kind of help or answer they were after.

- Code the **kind of help wanted**, not the health subject. The same type of request can be about any illness, symptom or medicine, and must not be split by subject. A separate codebook covers health topics.
- **Do not create a code for replying to, following up on, or reacting to the AI.** We are studying what people asked for at the start. If a message continues an earlier exchange, code what it asks for.
- No example categories are given on purpose. The types should come from the messages themselves.
- A message can show **more than one** type of request. Code every type that is clearly there.
- A type should recur: keep only types seen in at least 3 different messages. For 53 messages, roughly 5 to 8 types is a sensible size. Do not force a number.
- List any messages that fit none of your types, such as a greeting with no request, in `no_code_chats` with a reason.

For each type of request, give:

1. `name`: a short, plain-language name of 2 to 6 words.
2. `definition`: 1 to 3 sentences. The first sentence must stand on its own as the definition.
3. `signs`: 2 to 5 concrete signs in the message, such as typical phrasings or question forms.
4. `closest_other`: the name of your most similar type, and `how_it_differs` in one or two sentences, including how to decide between them.
5. `examples`: 2 or 3 example quotes from **different chats**, each with its `chat_id`. Each quote must be copied **exactly, character for character**, from a `[FIRST MESSAGE]` line: one continuous stretch of 3 to 40 words, or the whole message if it is shorter. Do not fix spelling, punctuation or capitals, and do not join separate pieces with "...".
6. `chat_ids`: every chat that shows this type. `n_chats` must equal the length of this list.

3. Merging the passes

For each codebook, a 4th fresh session read only the three pass outputs and the first messages (prompts/merge_prompt.md). It matched codes by meaning, not by name, and kept a code only if at least 2 of the 3 passes found it. Codes found by just one pass are listed below. Any the merger thought worth a second look are flagged for you to decide on.

dropped_all <- bind_rows(topic$dropped |> mutate(book = "Health topic"),
                         request$dropped |> mutate(book = "Type of request"))
if (nrow(dropped_all) > 0) {
  dropped_all |>
    mutate(worth_review = ifelse(worth_review %in% TRUE, "Yes", "")) |>
    select(book, dropped_by, pass, name, reason, worth_review) |>
    gt(groupname_col = "book") |>
    cols_label(dropped_by = "Dropped by", pass = "Pass", name = "Dropped code", reason = "Why",
               worth_review = "Worth your review?") |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = px(16), row_group.font.weight = "bold")
} else cat("No pass code was dropped.")

The merger’s notes (code IDs translated to the final numbering used in this report; a code you dropped is shown as [dropped: name]):

  • Health topic: The three passes agreed closely: seven topics (bones/joints, digestion, skin/allergies, infections, diet/weight, eyes, hormones/diabetes) appeared in all three, usually with the same examples. Differences were about how to split: pass 2 combined reproductive health with hormones and mental health with sleep; pass 3 had no headache/nerve-pain code and widened digestion to kidneys and liver. The merge follows the majority in each case, so no pass code was dropped. Boundaries to watch in the pilot: (1) PCOS and lists of mixed conditions (69f4ca1a) between Diabetes and hormones and Pregnancy and reproductive health; (2) headaches between Headaches and nerve pain and Infections and acute illness, and limb neuropathy between Headaches and nerve pain and Bones, joints and muscles; (3) perianal abscess (5d7fd2a5) between Stomach and digestion and Infections and acute illness; (4) tiredness inside a flu-like illness vs Sleep and fatigue; (5) hair growth on a GLP-1 drug (69fe1811) between Skin, hair and allergies and Diet, weight and fitness. Messages without a fitting topic in two or more passes: greetings or one-word replies (6ae359af, 6a9bb385), chest pain on exercise (671a8337), kidney ultrasound report (6a638cf5), child development (69c41892), and stress/anxiety or family emotional struggles (6a0206ae, 6929d658). Mental health was coded only by pass 2 (inside its sleep code); the researcher may want to consider a separate Mental health and stress topic if more such messages appear in the full data. Very short or context-dependent messages (66aafcc3, 6a24b2df) were coded weakly by all passes.
  • Type of request: Agreement was high: six codes (cause, relief, general facts, medical care, personal plan, information without a question) appeared in all three passes with closely overlapping chats; text tasks appeared in passes 1 and 2. Two pass-1-only codes were dropped. Unclear boundaries for the pilot: (1) R1 vs R2 when a personal symptom is followed by a general question (5f491a49, 6a10664c) - code both; (2) R3 vs R5 for ‘should I do X’ questions that are not about professional care (69d51123, drinking after surgery); (3) R2 vs R5 for what to expect at an appointment (6a106089); (4) R6 vs [dropped: Help with a text task] for 66fd6acd (incorporate an article into a wellness project); (5) R4 vs a possible results-interpretation code for pasted reports (6a638cf5, 66ec5904). Some first messages appear to continue an earlier exchange (66aafcc3, 67d5d3b7, 6a9bb385); per the dimension rules there is no code for replying to the AI, so code only any request content. Greetings with no request (6ae359af, 6a24b2df, 6a9bb385) should stay uncoded. Emotional support/talking through stress appeared once (6a0206ae) and was coded under R3 by all passes; watch for it in the pilot.

How a message is counted. Each pass placed messages under its own codes. For a merged code, a message counts if at least 2 of the 3 passes put it there. This majority vote means one pass’s odd call cannot add or remove a message. For topics, the primary topic is the one that at least 2 passes chose as primary. If the 3 passes chose 3 different primary topics, the message is marked “no majority”.

4. Changes made after the passes

Two kinds of change were made after the LLM passes. The passes were not rerun, because the codebooks are still drafts. Instead, the script 07c recounts everything with the changes applied, and each change is written down so it can be checked.

Exclusions

In step 05, 1 participant was flagged exclude = TRUE. Their paste was a homework assignment that happened to be about health (the AI summarised a CDC section on child development and wrote a class discussion post), not a personal health conversation. Their rows stay in the data, and the reason is recorded in output/05_build-conversation-dataset/05_exclusions.csv.

The 3 passes had already read this message, because they ran before it was excluded. So:

  • it is left out of every count, every kappa, every chart and every codebook example in this report, which therefore covers 52 first messages;
  • the pass input files are unchanged, so they still show exactly what the passes saw;
  • the table below records what each pass did with it, which shows what changed when it was removed.

Your review decisions

After reading the draft, you made the changes below. They are kept in a hand-made file, 07_codebook_revisions.csv, and applied by 07c after the majority vote. revisions |>

Mental health and stress now covers 2 chats. That is under the 3-chat minimum, but it is kept because you asked for it, and it is flagged as small in the tables. No other message without a topic clearly fits it. The rest are a greeting, a one-word reply, chest pain when running, and a kidney ultrasound report.

5. Checking the example quotes

Script: scripts/07_build-codebook/07c_check_and_build_codebook.py

LLMs can tidy up or invent quotes. So a script checked every example quote from all passes and both merges, plus the 2 quotes you chose for the new mental-health topic (“analyst”). Each quote had to appear word for word in the first message of the chat it is credited to. Only spacing was allowed to differ. The quotes from the excluded chat were checked too, but they are not used as examples in the codebooks.

quotes |>
  mutate(codebook = books[codebook]) |>
  group_by(codebook, source) |>
  summarise(quotes = n(), found_verbatim = sum(found_verbatim), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(result = ifelse(found_verbatim == quotes, "all found", "SOME NOT FOUND")) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "codebook") |>
  cols_label(source = "From", quotes = "Quotes", found_verbatim = "Found word for word", result = "") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(16), row_group.font.weight = "bold")

6. How well the passes agreed

How to read the tables below:

  • Found in passes: how many of the 3 passes came up with the code on their own.
  • Fleiss’ kappa: whether the passes put the same messages under the code, after removing the agreement you would expect by chance. 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level, and above about 0.6 is usually called good.
  • For topics, there is also one overall kappa for the primary topic, where each pass picks one topic per message:
    • kappa = 0.81;
    • all 3 passes chose the same primary topic for 75% of messages;
    • at least 2 agreed for 100%.
  • All kappas use the 52 analysed messages (the excluded chat is left out) and describe the passes before your review decisions. “Final count” includes those decisions. A code you added has no kappa (shown as a dash), because no pass found it.

Health topic

topic$agreement |>
  select(code, name, n_passes_found, primary_pass1, primary_pass2, primary_pass3, n_primary, n_chats, fleiss_kappa) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(code = "", name = "Topic", n_passes_found = "Found in passes",
             primary_pass1 = "Pass 1", primary_pass2 = "Pass 2", primary_pass3 = "Pass 3",
             n_primary = "Final count: primary", n_chats = "Final count: primary or secondary",
             fleiss_kappa = "Fleiss' kappa") |>
  tab_spanner("Primary topic in", columns = c(primary_pass1, primary_pass2, primary_pass3)) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(16))

topic_plot <- topic$agreement |>
  mutate(label = factor(paste0(code, " ", name), levels = rev(paste0(code, " ", name))),

7. Draft codebook 1: health topic

This is the part to review. For each topic, the table shows:

  • what it is and how to spot it;
  • how it differs from its nearest neighbour;
  • real examples, with the chat ID (the first 8 characters of the Prolific PID);
  • how many of the 52 first messages have it as their primary topic.

The same content is in 07_Q4_3_draft_codebooks.xlsx (sheet topic_codebook), where you can edit it.

codebook_gt(topic$codebook, function(d) paste0(d$n_primary, " primary<br>", d$n_chats, " primary or secondary"))
Code Definition Signs in the message How it differs Examples (chat ID)
T1. Bones, joints and muscles

9 primary
10 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about pain, injury, or a condition of the bones, joints, muscles, back, or neck. Includes knee, back, neck, foot, and elbow pain, arthritis, osteoporosis, bone density and fracture risk, and bony lumps.
  • names a joint, limb, back, or neck as the site of pain or injury
    - mentions arthritis, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, fractures, or bone density (DEXA) results
    - pain after walking, exercise, lifting, or an injury
    - asks what kind of joint or muscle injury something is
 vs. Headaches and nerve pain: Bones, joints and muscles covers pain arising from bones, joints, muscles, and the spine. Headaches and nerve pain covers headaches and pain described as nerve-related (for example neuropathy). If the message names neuropathy or nerve pain, use Headaches and nerve pain even if the pain is in a limb; if it describes joint, back, or muscle pain without naming nerves, use Bones, joints and muscles. Chest and abdominal pain are not part of this code. “what kind of knee injury does this sound like” (69fff128)

“i developed a sharp pain in my neck that raidates to my shoulders suddenly” (5aeeb490)

“symptoms of osteoarthrits” (663b8ae0)
T2. Diet, weight and fitness

6 primary
7 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about nutrition, body weight, exercise, or fitness goals. Includes healthy eating, protein and supplements for fitness, normal or ideal weight, fat loss, workouts, and weight-loss medicines such as GLP-1 drugs.
  • asks about healthy foods, meal plans, or protein intake
    - asks about normal or ideal weight, or losing fat or weight
    - mentions workouts, exercise, or fitness goals
    - mentions a GLP-1 or weight-loss medicine such as Zepbound
 vs. Diabetes and hormones: Diet, weight and fitness is about lifestyle goals around eating, weight, and exercise. Diabetes and hormones is about a diagnosed or suspected hormone or metabolic condition (diabetes, A1c, cholesterol, hormone imbalance). If the message is about diet or supplements to treat a named condition, code the condition as primary and this code as an optional secondary. “I want to discover affordable, healthy foods that will help me achieve my fitness and wellness goals.” (69a1ae3c)

“What is the normal weight for a male who is 28 and five feet nine inches tall?” (6952e59d)

“What impact (if any) has taking a GLP-1A medication had on your physical health?” (66c0f464)
T3. Stomach and digestion

6 primary
6 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about the stomach, bowel, anus, or other parts of the digestive tract. Includes stomach aches, belly or abdominal pain, gastritis, and anal or perianal problems such as fistulas.
  • stomach ache, tummy ache, or belly pain
    - names a digestive condition such as gastritis
    - pain or symptoms when using the bathroom
    - anal or perianal problems such as a fistula or perianal abscess
 vs. Infections and acute illness: Stomach and digestion is about a problem located in the digestive tract. Infections and acute illness is about sudden, whole-body illness or infection in general (fever, chills, body aches). If the main subject is a gut or anal problem, use Stomach and digestion even if infection is mentioned (an infection may be a secondary topic); if the message is about feeling generally ill or about infections in general, use Infections and acute illness. Weight and diet goals belong to Diet, weight and fitness. “I’ve been dealing with some bad stomach aches for the past few weeks.” (697cba85)

“Could it be gastritis? Tell me what causes gastritis and how long it can last.” (6a10664c)

“please list every disease where fistula-in-anu is a symptom” (6658d49a)
T4. Skin, hair and allergies

6 primary
6 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about the skin, scalp, or hair, or about allergic reactions. Includes eczema, hives, flaking or scabbing scalp, hair growth or loss, and allergies to foods or medicines such as antibiotics.
  • names a skin condition such as eczema, hives, or a rash
    - scalp flaking or scabbing, or hair growth or hair loss
    - asks about an allergic reaction or allergy to a food or drug
 vs. Infections and acute illness: Skin, hair and allergies covers surface skin and hair problems and allergic reactions. Infections and acute illness covers infections and short-term whole-body illness. An abscess or infection under the skin goes to Infections and acute illness (or the affected organ system); a rash, hives, or allergic reaction goes here. Hair changes while on a weight-loss drug go here, with Diet, weight and fitness as an optional secondary topic. “What does it mean if I have eczema dry spots on my skin” (6acb95ac)

“My scalp is flaking and scabbing” (672c1bfa)

“Can an allergic reaction appear slowly” (6a21a961)
T5. Infections and acute illness

4 primary
5 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about an infection or a sudden, short-term illness. Includes flu-like or cold symptoms (fever, chills, body aches, congestion), named infectious diseases such as hand foot and mouth disease, and questions about whether something is an infection.
  • sudden onset of feeling unwell with fever, chills, or body aches
    - asks what illness they caught or whether it is the flu
    - names an infectious disease or asks about infections in general
    - asks about an abscess or whether something is infected
 vs. Stomach and digestion: Infections and acute illness is about infection or sudden whole-body illness. If an infection is clearly located in one body system that has its own code (for example a perianal abscess), use that system’s code as primary and this code as secondary, or vice versa depending on which the message centres on. A headache on its own goes to Headaches and nerve pain; a headache that is one of several flu-like symptoms goes here. Tiredness that is part of a sudden flu-like illness goes here, not to Sleep and fatigue. “Today I suddenly started feeling bad, fatigue, body aches, felt hot, later had the chills, nose is congested. What did I catch?” (664639e0)

“What if hand foot and mouth isn’t treated” (6a637176)

“can infections of some sort smell like onions” (66d8e4c1)
T6. Diabetes and hormones

4 primary
5 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about diabetes, blood sugar, or another hormone or metabolic condition. Includes A1c results, diabetes, hormone imbalance, seeing an endocrinologist, testosterone, and cholesterol.
  • mentions diabetes, blood sugar, or an A1c value
    - asks about hormone imbalance or an endocrinologist
    - mentions testosterone or high cholesterol as a condition to manage
 vs. Pregnancy and reproductive health: Diabetes and hormones covers hormone and metabolic conditions in general. Pregnancy and reproductive health covers pregnancy, labor, periods, and female reproductive organs. PCOS can fit either: if the message centres on periods, fertility, or other reproductive conditions (such as PMDD or endometriosis), use Pregnancy and reproductive health; if it centres on hormones, blood sugar, or cholesterol, use this code; use the other as secondary when both are present. “72 yo woman with 6.0 a1c” (66ec5904)

“Would an endocrinologist benefit me from learning why my hormones are our of whack?” (6abae4ea)

“what diabetes” (6ad69d36)
T7. Sleep and fatigue

3 primary
4 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about sleep problems or ongoing tiredness. Includes poor or unrefreshing sleep, waking at night, sleep apnea, sleep loss, and fatigue, including sleep changes linked to a medicine.
  • asks about sleep apnea or snoring
    - waking during the night or trouble sleeping
    - feeling tired even after enough sleep
    - sleep changes after starting or changing a medicine
 vs. Infections and acute illness: Sleep and fatigue covers sleep problems and tiredness as the main subject. If tiredness is one of several symptoms of a sudden flu-like illness, use Infections and acute illness. Stress, anxiety, and emotional struggles are not part of this code (see notes). “I’ve been feeling unusually tired lately, even after getting a full night’s sleep.” (63e55f08)

“What is sleep apnea? I think I may have it.” (5f491a49)

“he’s been waking a lot in the night and he never used to do that.” (6144ea17)
T8. Eyes and vision

3 primary
3 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The message asks about the eyes or eyesight. Includes double vision, glasses, cataract surgery, and visits to eye doctors or retina specialists.
  • mentions vision changes such as double vision
    - mentions glasses, an eye doctor, or a retina specialist
    - asks about cataracts or eye surgery
 vs. Headaches and nerve pain: Eyes and vision is about the eyes themselves. Pain behind the eyes that comes with a headache or general illness goes to Headaches and nerve pain (or Infections and acute illness), not here. “Sometimes I’m not seeing double with my glasses on but sometimes I am.” (616f347d)

“My eye doctor is sending me to a retina specialist” (6a106089)

“Percentage of people need to get 2nd eye’s cataract surgery after doing the first one.” (69f441ce)
T9. Headaches and nerve pain

3 primary
3 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 2)		 The message asks about headaches or nerve pain. Includes headaches with or without other symptoms such as vomiting, and neuropathy or other pain described as coming from nerves.
  • says they have a headache or asks what to take for one
    - headache with vomiting or pain behind the eyes
    - mentions neuropathy or nerve pain
 vs. Bones, joints and muscles: Headaches and nerve pain covers headaches and pain named as nerve-related. Pain in a joint, muscle, back, or neck that is not described as nerve pain goes to Bones, joints and muscles. A headache that is one of several flu-like symptoms (fever, chills, body aches) goes to Infections and acute illness. “I have a headache, what should I take?” (69fd05bd)

“I have had an headache and vomitting for 2 days and pain behind my eyes” (6a9f047c)

“How to heal neuropathy pain in leg” (66d9e5be)
T10. Pregnancy and reproductive health

2 primary
3 primary or secondary
(passes 1, 3)		 The message asks about pregnancy, labor, menstruation, or the female reproductive organs. Includes labor and induction, periods, endometriosis, PCOS, and PMDD.
  • mentions pregnancy, labor, or induction
    - mentions periods or menstrual symptoms
    - names a reproductive condition such as endometriosis, PCOS, or PMDD
 vs. Diabetes and hormones: Pregnancy and reproductive health covers pregnancy and the female reproductive system. Diabetes and hormones covers hormone and metabolic conditions not tied to reproduction (diabetes, A1c, cholesterol, general hormone imbalance). When a message lists both kinds of conditions, code the one it centres on as primary and the other as secondary. “Should you be drinking 3 weeks after endometriosis surgery and about to have your period?” (69d51123)

“I want to deal with my pcos, anemia, pmdd, and high cholesterol” (69f4ca1a)
T11. Mental health and stress

2 primary
2 primary or secondary
(added by the analyst)
Small: under 3 chats		 The message is about the participant’s mental or emotional wellbeing: stress, anxiety, low mood, or emotional struggles in relationships or family life, rather than a physical symptom.
  • Words such as stressed, anxious, struggling, overwhelmed
    - Describes feelings or relationships rather than a body part or physical symptom
    - Asks how to cope or feel better emotionally
 vs. Sleep and fatigue: Sleep and fatigue is about sleep problems or physical tiredness; Mental health and stress is about emotional strain, stress or anxiety, even if tiredness is mentioned. “I just went a whole week without saying anything to my family.” (6929d658)

“I would like to talk about what’s stressing me out and why I’m anxious and what I can do to give myself a better quality of life.” (6a0206ae)

First messages with no topic

8. Draft codebook 2: type of request

The same layout. A message can have more than one type, so the counts add up to more than 52. The editable copy is the request_codebook sheet.

codebook_gt(request$codebook, function(d) paste0(d$n_chats, " messages"))
Code Definition Signs in the message How it differs Examples (chat ID)
R1. Ask what is causing symptoms

14 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant describes their own or someone else’s symptoms or health change and asks what could be causing it or what it means. The help wanted is an explanation or likely diagnosis for a specific personal situation.
  • “What could be causing this?” or “what could be the problem”
    - “What did I catch?” or “what kind of injury does this sound like”
    - “Could it be X or Y?” offering candidate causes
    - “Is that typical” or “Does that make sense?” about a described personal symptom
    - “How do I know if I have X”
 vs. General health facts: This code needs a personal case described in the message and a question about what is behind it. If the question is about a condition, medicine or procedure in general, use General health facts. A message can carry both (e.g. “Could it be gastritis? Tell me what causes gastritis”); code both. “Sometimes I wake up feeling like I haven’t rested at all. What could be causing this?” (63e55f08)

“nose is congested. What did I catch?” (664639e0)

“what kind of knee injury does this sound like” (69fff128)
R2. General health facts

14 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant asks for general information about a condition, symptom, test, procedure, medicine or health measure, not tied to explaining their own case. This includes definitions, symptom lists, causes, norms, statistics and likely outcomes.
  • “What is X?” or “symptoms of X”
    - “Can X …?” or “Does X …?” general yes-or-no fact questions
    - “List every …” or “Percentage of people …”
    - “What if X isn’t treated” or “what causes X and how long can it last”
    - “What will they do” at a test or appointment
 vs. Ask what is causing symptoms: General health facts asks how health works in general; Ask what is causing symptoms asks to explain a specific personal case. Decide by whether the question is about the person’s own described symptoms (code R1) or about a named condition or topic in general (code R2); code both if both are asked. “Can an allergic reaction appear slowly” (6a21a961)

“please list every disease where fistula-in-anu is a symptom” (6658d49a)

“What is the normal weight for a male who is 28 and five feet nine inches tall?” (6952e59d)
R3. Ask what to do for relief

8 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant asks what they (or the person they care for) can do, take or change to relieve, treat or manage a current health problem. The help wanted is practical self-care or treatment advice.
  • “What should I take?”
    - “What can I do to help/alleviate…”
    - “How to heal X”
    - “what do I do?” after describing a problem
    - “Would switching … help” about adjusting a current treatment
 vs. Whether to seek medical care: This code asks for self-care, medicine or habit steps to ease a problem. If the only choice being weighed is whether or when to see, call or use a professional or procedure, use Whether to seek medical care. If the request is goal-driven (fitness, nutrition) rather than problem-driven, use Personal plan or recommendations. “I have a headache, what should I take?” (69fd05bd)

“what can i do to alleviate knee pain and get back to normal?” (69fb8bf7)

“How to heal neuropathy pain in leg” (66d9e5be)
R4. Information shared without a question

8 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant states a symptom, health detail or test result with no explicit question or request, leaving the AI to infer what help is wanted (usually an assessment). This includes bare symptom phrases and pasted reports or lab values.
  • A short symptom phrase with no question, e.g. “CHEST PAIN WHEN RUNNING”
    - A statement about someone’s symptom or a noticed change, with no request
    - Age plus a test value, e.g. “72 yo woman with 6.0 a1c”
    - A pasted lab or imaging report with no request
 vs. Ask what is causing symptoms: Use this code only when no question or request is stated. If the message explicitly asks what is causing it, what it is, or what to do, code that request instead. “CHEST PAIN WHEN RUNNING” (671a8337)

“72 yo woman with 6.0 a1c” (66ec5904)

“Husband’s low back started hurting yesterday” (69600cc8)
R5. Whether to seek medical care

4 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant asks whether they should see a doctor or specialist, have a procedure, or contact their care team, or when to do so. The help wanted is a judgement on a specific decision about using professional care.
  • “Should I see a medical specialist … or try to wait it out?”
    - “Would an endocrinologist benefit me”
    - “Is it a must?” about a procedure
    - Checking when they can or should call the care team
 vs. Ask what to do for relief: This code is about a named decision to use (or not use) professional care, or its timing. If the person asks for self-care, medicine or habit steps, use Ask what to do for relief. A general question about what happens at an appointment is General health facts. “Should I see a medical specialist about this or try to wait it out?” (697cba85)

“Would an endocrinologist benefit me from learning why my hormones are our of whack?” (6abae4ea)

“Percentage of people need to get 2nd eye’s cataract surgery after doing the first one. Is it a must?” (69f441ce)
R6. Personal plan or recommendations

4 messages
(passes 1, 2, 3)		 The participant states personal wellness or fitness goals and asks for tailored recommendations, such as foods, meal ideas, supplements or a routine. The help wanted is a plan or product suggestion fitted to their goals, not treatment of a problem.
  • States goals such as fat loss, muscle gain or toning
    - Lists current diet, supplements, weight or budget
    - “Please recommend specific foods” or “suggest … ideas”
    - “Is there a supplement or vitamin that has …”
 vs. Ask what to do for relief: This code is goal-driven planning for diet, supplements or routine. If the focus is easing or treating a current symptom or problem, use Ask what to do for relief. “I want to discover affordable, healthy foods that will help me achieve my fitness and wellness goals.” (69a1ae3c)

“fat loss, muscle gain and increasing testosterone are the main objectives.” (69fcf529)

“Is there a supplement or vitamin that has fish oil, vitamin d3, vitamin c, B vitamins, magnesium, Berberine, and inositol?” (69f4ca1a)

First messages with no type of request

if (nrow(request$no_code) > 0) {
  request$no_code |>
    mutate(text = str_trunc(text, 300),
           why = coalesce(na_if(pass1_reason, ""), na_if(pass2_reason, ""), na_if(pass3_reason, ""), "")) |>
    select(chat_id, text, why) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(chat_id = "Chat", text = "First message (first 300 characters)", why = "A pass's reason") |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = px(16))
} else cat("Every first message has at least one type of request.")

9. What happens next

These are drafts. The plan stops here until you have reviewed them. The remaining steps are:

  1. Review and edit. Rename, merge, split or drop codes, and sharpen the definitions. Check the dropped codes marked “worth your review”. The codes with the lowest kappa in section 6 are the first ones to sharpen or merge.
  2. Pilot and freeze. Code the first messages with the edited codebooks, read the results, fix unclear rules, then freeze both codebooks.
  3. Code every first message 3 times. The LLM codes each first message with each frozen codebook three separate times, quoting its evidence. We keep each code that at least 2 of the 3 runs give.
  4. Hand-coding. You will hand-code all messages, and we will compare your codes with the LLM’s.

first_message_codes.csv already lists each message with its draft primary topic, secondary topic and types of request. It is a preview only, not final coding.

Limits to keep in mind

  • Small sample. There are 52 first messages. A code seen in 2–5 messages rests on very few people.
  • Pasted past chats. People chose what to paste. Some pastes may not start at the true first message of the conversation; in 2 of them, AI text comes first.
  • Lost line breaks. The export removed line breaks, so long first messages run together.

Files written

All in output/07_build-codebook/:

  • input/:
    • first_messages.csv (the 53 first messages, plus any AI context; the exclude column marks the excluded chat)
    • topic_pass_N_input.txt and request_pass_N_input.txt (the shuffled file each pass read)
    • pass_orders.csv (order and seed per pass)
    • redaction_log.csv
    • settings.json
  • passes/: <codebook>_pass_N_prompt.md (the exact prompt) and <codebook>_pass_N_raw_output.json (raw LLM output)
  • merge/: <codebook>_merge_prompt.md and <codebook>_merge_raw_output.json
  • Results:
    • 07_Q4_3_draft_codebooks.xlsx, with sheets topic_codebook, request_codebook, first_message_codes, overall_agreement, per-codebook agreement, no-code, dropped and pass codes, quote_check, and about
    • the same tables as CSVs
    • figures/
    • this report
  • Exclusions and review decisions:
    • 07_codebook_revisions.csv (hand-made list of your review decisions; edit it to change them)
    • codebook_revisions_applied.csv and excluded_chats.csv (also sheets in the workbook)
  • old_before-exclusion/: the workbook as it was before the exclusion and your review decisions.
  • old_all-messages/: the earlier all-messages draft. Its inputs and raw JSON contain names, so don’t share them.
